title: urgency-weighted-batching-field-notes
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a rough field-note doc capturing the urgency-weighted batching experiments we ran Nov 2025 -> Mar 2026. The idea: add a per-request urgency weight to the batch formation score so that requests with high urgency (interactive low-latency SLAs) can be preferentially flushed earlier while still preserving batch efficiency for background work. Goal was to reduce p99 tail without blowing up cost or harming p50 for bulk traffic.

High level conclusion (TL;DR):
- Urgency weighting reduced observed p99 by ~18–24% for mixed workloads (interactive + background) at modest throughput loss (~3–7% tokens/s depending on weight aggressiveness).
- The biggest practical friction was serialization + RPC contention on the CPU side when aggressive preemption/flushes were enabled; not GPU kernel time.
- Best sweet spot in our tests: urgency_scale=1.2, decay_window=250ms, min_batch_size=4 — yields ~20% p99 improvement and ~4% throughput loss vs baseline.

Background + motivation:
- Current continuous-batcher forms batches by age + size heuristics. It treats all in-flight requests equally which means background generation (longer generation requests, embeddings, larger context) can increase queueing variance for interactive requests that need low tail latency.
- We want a lightweight mechanism to give small urgency-based priority without hard priority queues (which can starve).
- Requirements: easy to tune, compatible with prefix caching/KV reuse, no per-request expensive ops, no extra GPUs.

Mechanism implemented (prototype):
- Each request carries urgency_weight in [0.5, 2.0] (default 1.0). mobile/web interactive requests: 1.3–1.6; background batch jobs: 0.6–0.9.
- Batch score = sum(1 / (age_ms * urgency_weight) ???) — note: prototype used a simpler effective "age*scale" ordering: effective_age = age_ms / urgency_weight (so higher urgency => larger effective age => flush sooner).
- Flushing rules: batch flush when effective_min_age > timeout_ms OR batch_size >= configured_min_batch_size OR GPU slot starvation threshold reached.
- Decay window: requests reduce urgency_weight over time linearly to avoid starvation when they linger (configurable decay ms).

Experiment setup:
- Cluster: 8-node cluster, each node 8x A100 40GB (internal test infra). Scheduler binary v0.62, runtime branch urgency-weighting-2025.
- Workloads: mixed-interactive (70% interactive, 30% background), mixed-heavy (50/50), background-heavy (30/70). Interactive trace from customer-sim 2025-10; background is long-gen synthetic (avg tokens 1200).
- Measurement window: 60 minutes steady-state per run, 3 warmup minutes. Captured per-request latencies, tokens/s, GPU utilization, host CPU p95/p99 syscall latencies, serialization times, and KV cache hit rates.

Key runs (representative runs, not exhaustive):
1) baseline (no urgency weighting)
- p50/p95/p99 latencies (interactive trace): 48ms / 150ms / 420ms
- tokens/s: 27k
- GPU utilization: 68% average
- CPU scheduler serialization avg: 1.9ms

2) urgency_scale=1.5, decay=500ms, min_batch_size=4
- p50/p95/p99: 50ms / 134ms / 325ms  (p99 -22%)
- tokens/s: 25.8k (-4.4%)
- GPU utilization: 65%
- Observed increase in host-side RPC calls (flushes) + serialization avg 2.5ms (up from 1.9ms)

3) urgency_scale=2.0, decay=250ms, min_batch_size=2 (aggressive)
- p50/p95/p99: 53ms / 128ms / 310ms (p99 -26%)
- tokens/s: 24.5k (-9.3%)
- GPU utilization: 61%
- CPU serialization up to 3.6ms under bursts; observed kernel launch frequency increase (smaller batches more often)

4) urgency_scale=1.1, decay=1000ms, min_batch_size=8 (conservative)
- p50/p95/p99: 49ms / 142ms / 370ms (p99 -11%)
- tokens/s: 26.6k (-1.4%)
- GPU utilization: 67%

Profiling notes and bottlenecks discovered:
- CPU-side serialization overhead: each additional flush increases CPU time spent packing requests and issuing RPCs. For aggressive urgency we saw CPU serialization jump, which eroded per-GPU throughput. This explains tokens/s drop more than expected from purely smaller batch math.
- RPC contention: more frequent flushes meant more concurrent gRPC calls to the node-local inference worker. We measured increased tail in gRPC send/recv on the host (syscall tail spikes correlated with p99 improvements fading).
- Kernel launch vs compute: GPU time per token actually decreased slightly with smaller batches (less efficient kernel occupancy), but kernel launch overhead did not dominate; CPU-side envelope dominated for the small batch sizes we tested.
- KV cache thrash: preemption of long-running requests sometimes forced KV caches to be re-warmed for urgent requests on different worker shards. This had a small but measurable penalty for interactive requests when model context reuse is high.

Observations on fairness/regression risk:
- Background jobs saw increased p99 and slower completion for aggressive urgency. In many customer contexts, background jobs are not latency-sensitive so this is acceptable, but SLA-sensitive batch jobs will be impacted.
- Without decay, low-urgency requests could be starved for long windows; decay prevented infinite deferral.
- When we combined urgency weighting with the admission-control batch-shaping we previously use, the combination prevented starvation while keeping p99 gains. (See linked PR for config knobs).

Operational complexity:
- Exposing urgency_weight to customers is too sharp; we should map request route -> urgency class server-side via routing rules (e.g., "interactive", "standard", "bulk").
- Default mapping: interactive routes get 1.2; background get 0.8. We tested a gradual ramp to avoid surprises.
- Telemetry we need: per-route urgency distribution, flush count per minute, serialization time histogram, and GPU batch-size distribution. Current console dashboards missing flush count metric; add to next sprint.

Sanity checks and verification steps we ran:
- Replayed interactive-only trace with high urgency to ensure no regression in p50 (it increased slightly due to more small batches).
- Verified that quantization/eager-weights path unchanged and model outputs unchanged (no quality regression).
- End-to-end correctness: no dropped tokens, no increase in failed requests attributable to urgency logic.

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Is there a hybrid approach that scores requests by both urgency and expected compute (tokens to generate) so we don't starve big-but-urgent jobs?
- Can we optimize CPU serialization path (e.g., vectorized packing or reuse of pre-allocated buffers) to recover throughput lost to frequent flushes?
- Would a tiny hardware-accelerated coalescer or local batching shim alleviate RPC contention? Research spike planned.

Next steps / recommended roadmap:
1) Short term (next 2 sprints)
- Add telemetry for flush count / flush-rate and per-route urgency histogram to Console. (owner: Emily)
- Implement pre-allocated batch packing buffers + micro-optimizations in the scheduler to reduce serialization GC churn. (owner: Priya)
- Roll out conservative default mapping (interactive 1.15, standard 1.0, bulk 0.85) behind feature flag; canary to 5% traffic. (owner: Marcus)

2) Medium term (quarter)
- Evaluate combining urgency weight with estimated remaining compute tokens to avoid penalizing long but urgent jobs. Prototype in simulator. (owner: Omar)
- Investigate admission-control integration to balance throughput targets with urgency windows. (owner: eng-serving-runtime)

3) Research / long term
- Explore an async coalescer shim (user-space Q-in-Q) that aggregates flushes locally to reduce gRPC churn.
- Study dynamic per-shard KV caching strategies to avoid rewarm during preemption.

Appendix: quick configs tried (for reproducibility)
- baseline: urgency_scale=1.0, decay_ms=inf, min_batch_size=8, flush_timeout_ms=80
- runA: urgency_scale=1.5, decay_ms=500, min_batch_size=4, flush_timeout_ms=60
- runB: urgency_scale=2.0, decay_ms=250, min_batch_size=2, flush_timeout_ms=40
- runC: urgency_scale=1.1, decay_ms=1000, min_batch_size=8, flush_timeout_ms=80

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working doc — numbers are median of a few runs and a/b runs; we should reproduce 2x with the production cluster before any customer-facing announcement.
- If you want the raw CSVs and perf traces I pushed them to the linked PR artifacts (see github pr).
